effect_estimate.comment: Quantitative descriptive results from an uncontrolled pre-post household survey of 463 OHOT beneficiary households (plus brief summary statistics cited from a separate 386-household third-party evaluation). Only descriptive percentages, means, and a gender comparison statement at the 5% significance level are reported (no confidence intervals or exact p-values).
effect_estimate.value: In Shelter Associates' ULB-partnered, GIS-targeted, cost-sharing 'One Home-One Toilet' (OHOT) program across 4 Maharashtra cities (N = 463 households / 2,263 individuals in Table 1), Community Toilet Block (CTB) reliance fell from 96.1% pre-intervention to 11.0% post-intervention among males and from 96.3% to 8.8% among females (Table 2); post-intervention, 91.2% of females and 89.0% of males used their household toilets (no significant gender difference in non-usage at the 5% level). Despite 72% of surveyed homes having floor area <250 ft2 (mean 208 ft2; Table 3), 72% built toilets inside the house and 28% built on a shared exterior wall. Under the phased material-delivery and labour cost-sharing mechanism, 99% of households reported satisfaction, spending a mean of Rs. 10,800 on toilet construction (~Rs. 8,000 labour; 58% [270/463 households] spent Rs. 10,800 or less), and 52.5% invested in further housing upgrades (mean total spend Rs. 23,500; Table 4). Routine monitoring of a 15% beneficiary sample indicated >90% toilet functionality/use beyond 6 months, and a cited third-party 1-year pre-post case-control evaluation (N = 386 households) found 93% family-wide toilet use, 100% adolescent girl use, and a drop in UTI symptoms from 23% to 13%.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Assigned '1' (documented descriptive association) under the JBI design ceiling (max '2'). The empirical survey (PDF pp. 3–6) provides descriptive pre-post and post-intervention household tabulations showing toilet uptake, CTB reduction, satisfaction (99%), and beneficiary co-payment levels (mean Rs. 10,800) among 463 households participating in the OHOT cost-sharing/facilitation model, while ULB spatial-data validation, SBM subsidy implementation struggles, and municipal governance coordination are described programmatically by the implementing NGO without direct empirical audit or comparative testing of municipal administrative processes.

mechanism_flags.comment: The paper examines GIS spatial slum/drainage mapping validated by Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) for targeted planning and SBM integration (ELIGIBILITY: planning), beneficiary labour cost-sharing vs direct subsidies (BURDEN: fees), community mobilization and women-led settlement sanitation committees (participation), NGO-ULB-government web data sharing and partnership (political_coordination), and hands-on vulnerability targeting and phased doorstep material facilitation (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: bureaucratic_assistance). Land tenure is mentioned only once in a general background sentence on PDF p. 1 and is not empirically analyzed.

outcome_flags.comment: Primary measured outcomes are individual household toilet construction/use versus open defecation and Community Toilet Block reliance (sanitation_access) and household out-of-pocket construction cost-sharing expenditure and willingness/capacity to pay (affordability). Program-level facilitation of ~15,000 toilets and >90% 6-month toilet functionality are also noted on PDF pp. 2–3.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The primary empirical analysis presented in Tables 1–4 (N = 463 beneficiary households) is an uncontrolled pre-post and cross-sectional post-intervention descriptive household survey without a non-intervention comparator group (thus not meeting ROBINS-I's genuine comparator requirement such as controlled before-after or DiD). Although PDF p. 3 briefly lists headline percentages from an external third-party 'pre-post case-control study' (N = 386), no comparator-group numbers, methods, or statistical models from that external study are reported in this paper.
